questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests building a robust, real-time workflow engine inside Kubernetes that handles idempotence, DAG scheduling, and observability in a scalable way.

## Key Concepts
- DAG orchestration in Kubernetes
- Event deduplication and idempotence
- Per-task retries with exponential backoff
- Finalizers and cleanup
- Observability (metrics, logs, traces)
- Security and RBAC for event sources and Jobs

## Code Example
```yaml
# CRD schema sketch for EventDrivenJob
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: eventdrivenjobs.k8s.example.com
spec:
  group: k8s.example.com
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                eventSource:
                  type: string
                dag:
                  type: array
                  items:
                    type: object
                    properties:
                      name:
                        type: string
                      dependsOn:
                        type: array
                        items:
                          type: string
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: eventdrivenjobs
    singular: eventdrivenjob
    kind: EventDrivenJob
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle late-arriving events that cause DAGs to be re-evaluated?
- How would you ensure idempotency if a TaskJob fails after success due to external mutation?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to orchestrate namespace-scoped apps with public exposure and TLS using cert-manager in a beginner-friendly context.

## Key Concepts

- Namespace isolation and minimal deployments
- Ingress with TLS via cert-manager
- ClusterIssuer/Issuer setup and annotations
- End-to-end validation with kubectl and basic health probes

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:stable-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  selector:
    app: web
```

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-alpha
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - example.com
    secretName: team-alpha-tls
  rules:
  - host: example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
```

```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: user@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress:
          class: nginx
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you scale to multiple namespaces with shared TLS resources?
- How would you rotate certificates and monitor expiry across namespaces?

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates real-world deployment experience, understanding of deployment strategies, and ability to handle production incidents that affect user experience.

## Expected Answer
The candidate should identify that rolling updates can cause performance degradation during transition periods, explain the benefits of canary deployments (gradual traffic testing, quick rollback capabilities), and discuss specific monitoring metrics (latency, error rates, resource utilization) and automation tools.

## Code Example
```yaml
# Canary deployment example
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: video-processing-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 50
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 100
      analysis:
        templates:
        - templateName: success-rate
        - templateName: latency
        args:
        - name: service-name
          value: video-processing-service
```

Blue/green deployment teaches safe, zero-downtime releases using Kubernetes primitives (Deployments, Services, Ingress) without advanced traffic tools.

- Separate Deployments and Services per version

- Smoke testing and rollback verification in CI

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-blue

    app: web
    version: blue

  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
      version: blue
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
        version: blue

      containers:

questions.explanation:
## Why This Matters

StartupProbe distinguishes slow-start containers from unhealthy ones, preventing rolling updates from stalling when container images require longer initialization time.

## Key Concepts

- **StartupProbe**: Runs at container startup; once it succeeds, readinessProbe takes over
- **ReadinessProbe**: Checks ongoing availability; only runs after startupProbe succeeds
- **failureThreshold × periodSeconds**: Determines maximum startup time (60 × 10s = 10 minutes maximum)

## Concrete Values

| Parameter | Value | Rationale |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| httpGet.path | /health/start | Application-specific startup endpoint |
| httpGet.port | 8080 | Match the container port |
| periodSeconds | 10 | Check every 10 seconds |
| failureThreshold | 60 | Allow up to 10 minutes for startup |

## Rollout Behavior

Without StartupProbe: Kubernetes treats slow-starting containers as failed during the initial probe window, causing rollout stalls and unnecessary restarts.

With StartupProbe: The deployment grants up to 10 minutes for the container to initialize. Once startupProbe succeeds, readinessProbe takes over for ongoing health checks. Rolling updates proceed smoothly without false failures.


## CI Verification Impact

- **Tests must**: Verify /health/start endpoint exists and returns 200 when ready
- **Verify**: StartupProbe config matches the expected initialization time
- **Adjust**: CI timeouts to account for the extended startup window
- **Monitor**: Check that readinessProbe activates after startupProbe succeeds
